title: SoA vs AoS
sub: Why memory layout matters more than it seems, and how Entities is built around it
cards/0/body:
A CPU doesn’t read one number from memory. It reads a cache line — 64 bytes on most modern CPUs (128 on Apple Silicon). Read one float, and its 15 neighbours land in L1 too.

A miss that goes all the way to RAM costs on the order of a hundred nanoseconds — hundreds of cycles in which SIMD code could have processed thousands of numbers. So in number crunching the speed is set not by the arithmetic but by how many useful bytes each line brings in.

The other ally is the prefetcher: on a sequential walk it loads the next lines ahead of time, and there are almost no misses. With random access by index it can’t help.

Hence the rule: the data a hot loop reads together should sit contiguous and dense, with no unrelated fields in between.
cards/1/body:
AoS (array of structures) is the familiar layout: a Unit struct with all its fields and a NativeArray<Unit>. The fields of one unit sit together, the units follow one another.

The movement loop reads the position and the velocity — 24 bytes — but a unit takes 52, and all 52 pass through the cache. More than half of every line is rotation, health and team, which this loop doesn’t need. Add more fields to Unit, and the loop gets slower even though its code didn’t change.

Vectorization suffers too. The x coordinates of neighbouring units are 52 bytes apart, so one instruction can’t load them: the compiler has to gather the numbers one by one or leave the code scalar.

AoS is good when an object is accessed as a whole and in random order: read one unit, and all its fields are in one or two lines.
cards/2/body:
SoA (structure of arrays) puts each field in its own array: positions, velocities, health… Element i is index i in all of them.

The movement loop now reads only two arrays, and every byte of every cache line is useful. The prefetcher follows two sequential streams, and neighbouring elements of one field sit side by side — exactly what SIMD needs.

NativeArray<float3> is a compromise: inside a float3, x, y and z are still together. For operations that treat all components the same way (pos += vel * dt) that hardly matters. If the formula mixes components (a length, a dot product), the fully split px, py, pz layout gives the compiler the easiest case: 8 x values in one ymm load.
cards/3/q: A pos += vel * dt loop over 100,000 units. Why is SoA faster than AoS?
cards/3/options/0: Only positions and velocities reach the cache, and neighbouring elements of one field are contiguous: full cache lines and SIMD
cards/3/options/1: There are more arrays, and the Job System hands them to different worker threads
cards/3/options/2: SoA takes less memory than AoS
cards/3/options/3: Burst can’t handle structs inside a NativeArray
cards/3/explain: The byte count is the same, but the loop touches only what it needs: 24 bytes per unit instead of 52, and the lines are filled with useful data. On top of that, neighbouring values of one field load with a single SIMD instruction.
cards/3/wrong/1: Threads split the indices, not the arrays: in AoS and SoA alike each thread takes its own batch of i.
cards/3/wrong/2: The total amount of data is the same — the same fields, just laid out differently.
cards/3/wrong/3: Structs in a NativeArray are normal for Burst; the only question is how many wasted bytes go through the cache.
cards/4/title: Lay out by access, not by class
cards/4/body:
SoA doesn’t mean “every field separate at any cost”. Group fields by who reads them and how often: hot (position and velocity — movement and collisions every frame), warm (health and cooldown — AI a few times a second), cold (the name — UI and save games). This is called a hot/cold split.

The price of SoA: more arrays, which have to be passed to the job together; removing an element means RemoveAtSwapBack in every array, or the indices drift apart; the code reads worse than unit.health. And reading all the fields of one object touches several lines in different arrays — for random access to a single unit, AoS can be faster.

The rule: pick the layout for the hot loops. If a loop over 100,000 elements reads 2 fields out of 10, go SoA. If the code takes one object and reads everything, stay AoS.
cards/5/q: What do you pay for SoA? Pick all that apply.
cards/5/options/0: Removing an element has to be repeated in every array, or the indices drift apart
cards/5/options/1: Reading all the fields of one object touches several cache lines in different arrays
cards/5/options/2: The Job System can’t split a job with several arrays into batches
cards/5/options/3: SoA is always slower than AoS if the loop reads more than one field
cards/5/explain: Keeping the indices in sync is your job: forget RemoveAtSwapBack in one array, and a unit gets someone else’s velocity. And random access to one object in SoA is smeared across several lines. The Job System splits index batches the same way whatever the number of arrays, and a loop that reads two or three fields out of many is exactly where SoA wins.
cards/6/body:
Entities is SoA out of the box. The set of component types of an entity is its archetype. Entities of one archetype live in 16 KiB chunks, and inside a chunk each component type has its own dense array, plus an array of the entity ids themselves.

A system that reads LocalTransform and Velocity walks exactly two arrays in each chunk and doesn’t pull health, AI or any other component into the cache. It’s the same SoA, just by component rather than by single field. Removing an entity moves the chunk’s last element into the freed slot — the same swap-back.

Inside a component it’s AoS: the fields of one struct sit together. That’s why components are kept small and split by access: what’s read together goes into one component, what’s rarely needed into another.

In the interview: “Entities stores components by type in chunks, so a job reads only the arrays it needs, contiguously, and Burst vectorizes it.”
cards/7/q: Match the layout to how the data sits
cards/7/pairs/0/1: All fields of one object together
cards/7/pairs/1/1: One field of all objects in a row
cards/7/pairs/2/1: An array per component type inside 16 KiB
cards/7/pairs/3/1: Frequent fields apart from rare ones
cards/8/task: Move MoveJob from AoS to SoA: instead of NativeArray<Boid>, two fields — NativeArray<float3> positions (read and written) and NativeArray<float3> velocities with [ReadOnly]. In Execute, move positions[i] by velocities[i] * dt. Keep the [BurstCompile] attribute.
cards/8/checks/0/label: There is a NativeArray<float3> positions field
cards/8/checks/1/label: There is a NativeArray<float3> velocities field with [ReadOnly]
cards/8/checks/3/label: Execute increases positions[i] by velocities[i] * dt
cards/8/explain: A Boid takes 44 bytes, and movement needs 24: after the split only positions and velocities go through the cache, while colour and flock stay in their own arrays. [ReadOnly] on velocities tells the safety system that other jobs may read the array in parallel. In the interview: “SoA so the compiler can vectorize — I check the Burst Inspector.”
cards/9/q: A 64-byte component was added to the unit archetype. The movement system reads only LocalTransform and Velocity. What changes for it?
cards/9/options/0: It reads the same arrays, but fewer entities fit into a 16 KiB chunk — more chunks, more per-chunk overhead
cards/9/options/1: It becomes about twice as slow: the new component goes through the cache too
cards/9/options/3: A structural change happens every frame
cards/9/explain: The useful bytes are the same: the LocalTransform and Velocity arrays are dense, other components sit in their own arrays and stay out of the cache. But a fixed-size chunk is shared by all the archetype’s components, so there are fewer entities per chunk and more chunks. Usually a small cost, but heavy, rarely used data gets moved out of the hot archetype.
cards/9/wrong/1: Components sit in the chunk as separate arrays; the system never touches the new component’s array.
cards/9/wrong/2: The chunk capacity went down, so there are more chunks — there is a little overhead.
cards/9/wrong/3: A structural change is adding a component to an entity, not reading. The archetype here is already like that.
cards/10/q: Interviewer: “A NativeArray<Enemy> with 20 fields, and a job that only moves positions every frame. What do you suggest, and how do you check it?”
cards/10/options/0: Move positions and velocities into separate arrays (a hot/cold split), compare the job time in the Profiler, and check in the Burst Inspector whether the instructions turned packed
cards/10/options/1: Increase batchSize so each thread takes more enemies
cards/10/options/2: Make Enemy a class so the 20 fields aren’t copied
cards/10/explain: The problem is bytes: the loop drags 20 fields through the cache for the sake of two. Splitting by access fixes it, and the Profiler and the Burst Inspector confirm it: the job time drops, and the loop body shows ps instructions instead of ss.
cards/10/wrong/1: batchSize changes how work is spread across threads, not how many wasted bytes each element carries.
cards/10/wrong/2: Classes aren’t allowed in Burst, and an array of references would also scatter the objects across the heap.
cards/10/wrong/3: A job’s container fields are already treated as non-overlapping; aliasing has nothing to do with it.
